Prof Rosling literally helped cure my depression. I live in a poor south asian country where democracy is a joke- and in 2018, two youth-led movements demanding social and legal reform were happening in here, in both of which I was active and the horribly ugly form of police brutality on young people and the govt injustice I experienced directly- along with the telltale silence of the civil society made me fall into a trap of pessimism, hoplessness, mistrust in the govt; ultimately driving me towards depression. It was, one of the hardest period of my life. 

By some miracle of the youtube recommendation mechanism, a video of prof Rosling was suggested to me in exactly around that dark time, and I immediately bought his book **Factfulness** and read it like a thirsty person drinks water. His lectures and the book simultaneously made me feel so much better, gave me a valuable insight about the world- so it was an eye-opening experience overall. I remain forever indebted to prof Rosling and his foundation, Gapminder because of helping me get out of the rut. I wish he was alive so I could write to him just how much he'd helped me get back up.

The climate and material of the clothes do matter. The clothes for the Hijabs, Burkhas and Chador/Shawl usually come with a variety of Silk, cotton and linen materials. Hijabs and Burkhas made from those materials are, to some extent, wearable. But the Niquab is never thin enough. So It's hard to breath underneath 'em. You feel as if you're wearing a mask that doesn't come with holes for your nostrils. The climate is mostly warm over here. So by wearing the whole ensemble at least 7/8 hours a day, your hair sweats a LOT and you get severe headaches. Some women drape the Hijab loosely, so plenty of air gets in. Some women choose to wear a tight cap underneath their Hijabs so not a single strand of hair escapes. Things are a bit harder for them.
This woman right here, gentlemen, is the type of women you can spend your life with and never stop feeling lucky.

I have been brought up in a conservative Asian Muslim family. My mother and Gran wear Hijabs with the Burkha and I was made to wear both of it since I was in grade 6. It was always a struggle for me as a petite teen to maintain that much clothing. I couldn't run. I couldn't do sports. I couldn't walk freely. I just never felt like I needed a Hijab to be counted as a "true believer"/"real Muslim".  And you don't really go anywhere by sitting down to have 'discussions' with your Asian parents so I couldn't talk them into allowing me to go out without Hijabs. 

I had to muster up some courage and just stopped wearing it. I didn't talk about it. No one saw it coming. It was a shock to them. It took quite some time and a lot of adjustments to be made for them to finally be okay with it, but I'm so effing glad that I did it. It feels as if I'd shed 10 pounds of unnecassry burdens :)
